definition: Defile means to make something unclean or impure.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word defile. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know defile should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A single afternoon of dye-dumping upstream defiled the pools where the town has always swum.
Dirty is far milder than defile — mud on boots, dust on sills, and a rinse undoes it; what defiles gets into the thing itself and does not rinse away.
Poison goes further than defile — defiled water is unfit to drink; poisoned water does harm with every swallow.

Pollute is defiling at environmental scale — rivers, air, whole coastlines fouled, usually measured in tons. Defile can strike one spring or one jar of honey, and it adds a note of offense that the laboratory report leaves out.

A taint is the smallest dose of the same uncleanness — one drop of dirt, or of doubt, in something otherwise clean, and a trace is all it takes. To defile goes all the way: the whole thing made impure, and the word rings with offense.
drive the uncleanness back out
wash clean, body or soul

The trampling verb behind defile never settled in English, and the -file you see is a costume borrowed from foul and filth. Peel the word and nothing usable is left — just remember it has nothing to do with files, nail or paper.
Defile means to make something unclean or impure.
The beekeeper's deal with the co-op turns on one word: pure.
Her hives sit two miles from the nearest field for a reason.
The summer a neighbor's sprayer drifted, the tests came back speaking of traces — nothing you could see, nothing you could taste — and the whole season's honey was refused.
What drift defiles, no filter recovers, because what entered is in the thing now, not on it.
Defile is the exact word for what happened to that honey, because it means to make something unclean or impure — and it carries a note of offense, as if the purity had been owed protection.
Contaminate states the laboratory fact; defile adds the sense that something kept clean has been wronged.
Defile is charged: it treats cleanness as something owed protection, which is why it suits springs, snowfields, and honey jars better than lab benches — there, contaminate is the plain term.
Its unit mates split the territory: deface attacks a surface's look, desecrate a place's sacredness, debase a thing's worth.
And despite its spelling, defile has nothing to do with filing anything.
